questions.prompt: Why should a fine-tuning benchmark include the **untuned base model**, served the same way as the fine-tuned model?

options.text: Because the base model is usually the cheapest option to deploy.
options.rationale: Cost is a separate axis. The base model is in the benchmark as a control.

options.text: It isolates what fine-tuning contributed: the gap between base and tuned on identical serving is the adapter's effect.
options.rationale: Yes. Without the control, a reader can't tell whether the training run did anything beyond what the base model already did.

options.text: Because public leaderboards require it.
options.rationale: Leaderboards have nothing to do with it. It's experimental design.

options.text: To provide a second frontier-model comparison.
options.rationale: The base model is small. It controls for the adapter, not for frontier capability.

questions.explanation: A comparison needs a control. Holding the model, engine, precision, and decoding constraint fixed and toggling only the adapter tells you how much the adapter itself changed quality.

questions.prompt: Scoring follows the lesson's rules: strings are stripped and casefolded, and a `None` prediction is wrong. What does this print?
questions.code:
def norm(v):
    return v.strip().casefold() if isinstance(v, str) else v

gold = ["Priya", None, "Sam", "Ana"]
pred = [" priya", None, None, "Dana"]
print(sum(norm(p) == norm(g) for p, g in zip(pred, gold)) / len(gold))

options.rationale: Null against null counts as correct: the model correctly abstained.
Yes. Case 1 matches after normalization, case 2 is null against null, cases 3 and 4 are wrong: 2 of 4.
Case 3 predicts null where the gold owner is Sam. That's a missed value, so it's wrong.
The denominator is all four cases. Nothing is dropped.

questions.explanation: Normalization handles formatting (case, whitespace), a correct abstention matches a gold null, and a missed or wrong value is an error. The denominator never shrinks.

questions.prompt: This function computes a system's exact-match rate. What is the problem with it?

options.text: Comparing dicts with `==` is unreliable in Python.
options.rationale: Dict equality compares keys and values, which is what exact match needs (normalization aside).

options.text: It should use the median instead of the mean.
options.rationale: Exact match is a proportion; the mean of 0/1 scores is the right estimator.

options.text: It drops unparseable outputs from the denominator, so a system that fails to produce valid JSON more often looks better.
options.rationale: Yes. Failures are wrong answers and must stay in the count.

options.text: `zip` will raise an error if the lists differ in length.
options.rationale: `zip` silently truncates, which is a second risk, but not an error.

questions.explanation: Two lessons hide in this function. Filtering out `None` rewards the system that fails most. And `zip` silently truncates mismatched lists, which is why the lab checks ids and the test-set fingerprint before scoring.

questions.prompt: Your fine-tuned model beats the frontier model by 19 points of exact match, far more than you expected. Training examples were generated by a frontier model from your company's transcripts, and the test set was labeled later from the same transcript archive. What is the best next step?

options.text: Check for contamination: identify which meetings the test cases came from, whether any were used to seed training data, and run a similarity check between training and test inputs.
options.rationale: Yes. If test meetings fed data generation, rebuild the test set from meetings excluded from every training step.

options.text: Report the result; a large margin is strong evidence.
options.rationale: A surprising margin is the classic symptom of contamination. Check before reporting.

options.text: Re-run the frontier model with a better prompt until the gap closes.
options.rationale: Tuning one side's prompt against the test set creates a different bias. The question is whether the test is clean.

options.text: Add more training data to widen the gap further.
options.rationale: The issue is the validity of the measurement, not the size of the effect.

questions.explanation: Contamination inflates the fine-tuned model specifically, because it is the system trained on your data. Split by source document, freeze the test set before generating training data, and keep a similarity check as a backstop.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in a self-hosted model's **cost per 1,000 tasks** calculation, or alongside it in the report? Select all that apply.

options.text: GPU hourly price, including hours when no requests arrive
options.rationale: Yes. Rented GPUs bill while running.

options.text: Throughput measured at the concurrency you will actually serve
options.rationale: Yes. Throughput depends heavily on batching, so it must be measured, not assumed.

options.text: The utilization you expect, stated explicitly
options.rationale: Yes. At 20 percent utilization, cost per task is five times the busy-GPU figure.

options.text: The API provider's per-token prices
options.rationale: Those apply to the API system, not the self-hosted one.

options.text: A note on operations and maintenance effort not captured per task
options.rationale: Yes. Engineering time, monitoring, and retraining are real costs even if you don't price them.

questions.explanation: Self-hosted cost per task is the GPU's hourly price divided by the useful tasks completed per hour. Both terms of that ratio are easy to flatter, so measure throughput and state utilization, and name the fixed costs that sit outside the formula.

questions.prompt: What is the main idea behind **continuous batching** in engines such as vLLM?

options.text: Requests are processed one at a time, continuously, to minimize latency.
options.rationale: That is no batching at all, and it wastes most of the GPU during decode.

options.text: The model is fine-tuned continuously on incoming requests.
options.rationale: Serving doesn't change the model's weights.

options.text: All prompts are concatenated into one long sequence.
options.rationale: Sequences are kept separate; they share decode steps, not context.

options.text: When any sequence in the running batch finishes, a waiting request takes its slot at the next decode step.
options.rationale: Yes. Scheduling per step keeps the GPU full instead of waiting for the longest sequence in a static batch.

questions.explanation: Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, so adding sequences to a step is cheap. Continuous batching exploits that by refilling slots as soon as they free up, which is a large part of why a busy server is so much cheaper per token than an idle one.

The second call fails the best-case check: even a fully used GPU costs more per task than that API.

questions.explanation: Volume can only rescue self-hosting if the GPU's best-case cost per task is below the API's. Against cheap API models it often isn't, which is why you compare against the cheapest model that passes your benchmark.

questions.prompt: Your team benchmarked the fine-tuned model in 16-bit precision on vLLM with schema-constrained decoding. To fit a cheaper GPU, an engineer proposes deploying a 4-bit GGUF version on llama.cpp. What should happen before it goes to production?

options.text: Nothing; quantization is lossless at 4 bits for models this size.
options.rationale: Quantization is lossy, and the loss depends on the model, method, and task.

options.text: Check its perplexity on a public benchmark.
options.rationale: General benchmark numbers won't tell you how it handles your fields and conventions.

options.text: Treat it as a new system: run the frozen benchmark with the same schema constraint, report the paired difference against the 16-bit version, and keep it only if it stays within the pre-registered margin.
options.rationale: Yes. The precision, engine, and constraint all changed, so the approved numbers no longer describe it.

options.text: Spot-check five outputs by eye.
options.rationale: Five outputs can't detect a few-point drop. Use the benchmark you already have.

questions.explanation: A benchmark describes one configuration. Change the precision, engine, or decoding constraint and you are serving an unmeasured system. Re-running the frozen benchmark is cheap and is the only evidence the deployed system is the one you approved.

questions.prompt: Read this DPO loss for one preference pair. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The loss is minimized by making the chosen response's absolute probability as high as possible, regardless of the reference.
options.rationale: The loss depends on log-ratios to the reference, not on absolute probabilities.

options.text: Raising beta makes the policy free to move further from the reference.
options.rationale: Higher beta ties the policy more tightly to the reference; TRL describes it as less deviation.

options.text: If the policy is identical to the reference, the loss is log 2 regardless of the probabilities.
options.rationale: Yes. Both log-ratios are zero, so the margin is zero and log(1 + e^0) is log 2.

options.text: The function needs a separately trained reward model as input.
options.rationale: That's the point of DPO: the reward is implicit in the policy and reference log-probabilities.

questions.explanation: `log1p(exp(-m))` equals minus log sigmoid(m), the DPO loss. The trained model is rewarded for preferring the chosen response more than the reference did, which is why a model that hasn't moved sits at log 2.

questions.prompt: You want a small extraction model and plan to distill it from a frontier model's outputs on 5,000 internal transcripts. Which plan is soundest?

options.text: Generate the outputs, train on all of them, and report the student's agreement with the teacher on a held-out set as its accuracy.
options.rationale: Agreement with the teacher measures imitation, including the teacher's errors, not correctness.

options.text: Skip verification; the teacher is a frontier model, so its outputs are effectively gold labels.
options.rationale: Frontier models still invent owners and dates. The student will learn those errors faithfully.

options.text: Distill from two different frontier models and keep only outputs where they agree, with no other evaluation.
options.rationale: Agreement filtering can help as one check, but it is not an evaluation, and shared errors pass through.

options.text: Check the provider's terms with your legal team first, verify the teacher's outputs with your extraction checks and a human-labeled sample before training, and evaluate the student on a human-labeled frozen test set.
options.rationale: Yes. Terms first, verified training data, and human-labeled evaluation.

questions.explanation: Distillation works well on narrow tasks when the data is verified and the evaluation uses human labels. Gudibande and colleagues showed what happens otherwise: students that copy style without capability. And providers' terms restrict training on outputs, so that question comes first.
